title.text: Measuring a model: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC and AUC, thresholds, baselines, overfitting

objects.text: How do I know whether a model is any good, and what should I ask the vendor who says it is?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 3 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Session 2 ended on a warning: a vendor's single high score means little until you know how it was tested. Today we test the tests. A smoke alarm teaches the vocabulary, then you see it on a real result table, you move a threshold yourself, and you meet a model that scores ninety percent by doing nothing.

The question for today is this: How do I know whether a model is any good, and what should I ask the vendor who says it is? Keep it in mind. At the end of the session we come back to it and see how much more you can say.

slides.notes:
That question breaks into three things you can do by the end of today. You can read a confusion matrix and work out accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from it. You will spot three ways a model looks good without being good: accuracy with no baseline, one number that hides the threshold, and overfitting.

And you leave with a one-page question sheet that you can put to any vendor, about the numbers behind their claim. There are no tests today. We use pencil and paper in the second half.

title.text:
Your two hours: a smoke alarm, then a real
result table, then your own pencil work

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_4f3a509d.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: The invoice numbers come from a run recorded in advance. Ask me to rerun it live.

slides.notes:
To get there, here is how the two hours run. We start with a smoke alarm, because everyone knows what it means for an alarm to ring when there is no fire, or to stay silent when there is one. That one example teaches the confusion matrix, precision, recall, the threshold, the baseline and F1.

A spam filter teaches overfitting. Then I apply the same ideas to a made-up late-payment model for Nile Valley Foods and run two demonstrations, moving the threshold while you watch the numbers change. After the break you work with a pencil on twenty cases and fill in a confusion matrix by hand.

We finish with the question sheet you can put to any vendor.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
2.  How does a decision tree reach its answer?
3.  How does a k-nearest neighbours model decide?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 2. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Supervised learning uses examples with the right answer (the label) attached, such as emails marked spam or not spam. Unsupervised learning is given no labels and finds groups.

Question two. How does a decision tree reach its answer? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. It asks a chain of yes or no questions about the features of the case, from the top down, until it reaches a leaf that gives the answer. The questions are learned from the training data.

Question three. How does a k-nearest neighbours model decide? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. It finds the k training examples most like the new one, using a distance, and gives the answer most of them had.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold training, validation and test data from Session 0 and a decision tree that can overfit from Session 2. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: confusion matrix, threshold, baseline, overfitting.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 4: turning words into numbers we can measure. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A table that counts the four kinds of outcome of a classifier: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.
Precision: of the cases flagged, the share that were real. Recall: of the real cases, the share that were flagged.
The score at or above which the model says positive. You choose it.
A simple reference model to beat, such as the majority-class baseline that always predicts the most common class.
ROC: a curve that shows every threshold at once. AUC: the area under that curve, one number between 0.5 and 1.
The model fits its training data, noise included, and does worse on new data. Memorising is the plain way to say it.

slides.notes:
6 words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Confusion matrix. A table that counts the four kinds of outcome of a classifier: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

Precision and recall. Precision: of the cases flagged, the share that were real. Recall: of the real cases, the share that were flagged.

Threshold. The score at or above which the model says positive. You choose it.

Baseline. A simple reference model to beat, such as the majority-class baseline that always predicts the most common class.

ROC curve and AUC. ROC: a curve that shows every threshold at once. AUC: the area under that curve, one number between 0.5 and 1.

Overfitting. The model fits its training data, noise included, and does worse on new data. Memorising is the plain way to say it.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
A confusion matrix counts four outcomes,
and a smoke alarm shows each one

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_alarm_7.70x4.80_8c07a6d3.png
objects.alt: A confusion matrix counts four outcomes, and a smoke alarm shows each one

objects.text: Invented numbers: 1,000 kitchen events, 20 real fires.

slides.notes:
We start with something everyone knows: a smoke alarm in a kitchen. Over one thousand events, twenty were real fires. The alarm rang sixteen times for a real fire. That is a true positive: the alarm said yes, and yes was right. It rang thirty-four times with no fire, perhaps for burnt toast.

That is a false positive, a false alarm. It stayed silent four times when there was a real fire, a false negative, the dangerous one. And it stayed silent nine hundred and forty-six times when all was well, a true negative. The table that counts these four outcomes is called a confusion matrix.

Every classifier has one. These numbers are invented for the lesson. Which box worries you most?

title.text:
Precision and recall ask two different
questions about the same alarm

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_alarm_7.70x4.80_8c07a6d3.png
objects.alt: Precision and recall ask two different questions about the same alarm

objects.text: Same matrix, three different questions.

slides.notes:
Now two divisions on that matrix. Precision asks: when the alarm rings, how often is there a real fire?

That is the true positives, sixteen, divided by everything it rang for, true positives plus false positives, fifty. Sixteen over fifty is thirty-two percent. Recall asks: of all the real fires, how many did it ring for?

Sixteen divided by true positives plus false negatives, twenty. That is eighty percent. Statisticians call recall the true positive rate. Accuracy is the share of all right answers, true positives plus true negatives, nine hundred and sixty-two out of a thousand, ninety-six point two percent. As an analogy, a very jumpy alarm rings for toast and for fires.

Its recall is high and its precision is low. Where the analogy breaks: a model has no feelings, only these counts.

title.text:
A baseline is the score to beat: the majority
class makes a silent alarm 98% accurate

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_alarm_base_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A baseline is the score to beat: the majority class makes a silent alarm 98% accurate

objects.text: The majority-class baseline always predicts the most common class: no fire.

slides.notes:
Here is the first way a model can look good without being good. Imagine an alarm that never rings. In our thousand events, nine hundred and eighty had no fire, so it is right nine hundred and eighty times: ninety-eight percent accurate. It beats our real alarm on accuracy, at ninety-six point two.

Yet it misses every fire, so its recall is zero. A simple reference model like this is called a baseline, and always predicting the most common class is the majority-class baseline. Any real model must beat the baseline on the measure that matters. When the thing you look for is rare, accuracy rewards doing nothing.

What is rare in your business?

title.text:
The threshold is the smoke level at which the alarm
rings, and moving it trades one error for the other

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_alarm_thr_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The threshold is the smoke level at which the alarm rings, and moving it trades one error for the other

objects.text: The threshold is the score at which the model says positive. You choose it.

slides.notes:
So far the alarm either rang or it did not. In fact an alarm measures smoke level, a score, and rings when the score reaches a line. That line is the threshold. The grey curve shows the smoke level at normal events like cooking. The red curve shows real fires.

They overlap, so no line is perfect. Raise the threshold and the alarm rings less: fewer false alarms, more missed fires. Lower it and the reverse. On our counts, a high threshold catches twelve of the twenty fires with eight false alarms. A low one catches nineteen with a hundred and eighty-one false alarms.

Choosing the threshold is a decision about costs. The model cannot make it for you.

title.text:
F1 score gives one number for precision
and recall, and punishes a lopsided pair

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_f1_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: F1 score gives one number for precision and recall, and punishes a lopsided pair

objects.text: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It stays near the weaker one.

runs.text: F1 = 2 × P × R ÷ (P + R), P precision, R recall.

slides.notes:
Two numbers are awkward when you want to compare alarms or models, so people squeeze them into one. The plain average is generous to a lopsided pair. Take precision ninety percent and recall ten percent: the average is fifty, which sounds middling, yet it misses nine of ten real cases.

F1 is the harmonic mean, a kind of average that stays close to the weaker number. The formula is two times precision times recall, divided by precision plus recall, which is two divided by one over precision plus one over recall. For that pair F1 is eighteen percent.

For our alarm, precision thirty-two and recall eighty, F1 is forty-six, below the average of fifty-six. F1 hides what each mistake costs, which we come to later.

title.text:
The five formulas in one place,
with the smoke alarm numbers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_formulas_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The five formulas in one place, with the smoke alarm numbers

objects.text: Invented alarm numbers: TP 16, FP 34, FN 4, TN 946. Gold: the formulas.

slides.notes:
Here are the five calculations on one page, because you will meet them in every vendor report. Say them aloud. Accuracy is true positives plus true negatives, over everything. Precision is true positives over true positives plus false positives. Recall, which statisticians call the true positive rate or sensitivity, is true positives over true positives plus false negatives.

The false positive rate is false positives over false positives plus true negatives: thirty-four false alarms out of nine hundred and eighty quiet events, three point five percent. We need it for the ROC curve. F1 is two times precision times recall, over precision plus recall. TP, FP, FN and TN are only the four counts in the matrix.

Which of these would a vendor most like to quote?

title.text:
Overfitting: a spam filter that memorised
its training emails does worse on new ones

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_versus_7.70x4.80_635974be.png
objects.alt: Overfitting: a spam filter that memorised its training emails does worse on new ones

objects.text: The model fits its training data, noise included, and does worse on new data. Invented numbers.

runs.text: Training set: what it learns from.
Test set: kept back to judge it.
A big gap is the warning.

slides.notes:
The third way to look good is overfitting. Think of a spam filter. It learns from two thousand example emails, the training set. If it simply memorises those exact emails, word for word, it scores one hundred percent on them. Then new spam arrives with different words, and the filter fails on it.

So we keep a test set, emails the filter never saw during learning, and judge it only on those. This is the plain meaning of overfitting: the model has fitted its training data, including its accidents, so it does worse on new data. The numbers on the slide are invented for the illustration. We will see a real case with decision trees shortly.

title.text:
Now the business case: a late-payment model gives
each invoice a score, and you choose the threshold

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_hist_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Now the business case: a late-payment model gives each invoice a score, and you choose the threshold

objects.text: Flag invoices likely to be paid late. Test set: 900 invoices, 83 late.

runs.text: Late invoices score higher, but the groups overlap.

slides.notes:
Now the same ideas on business data. A customer message is short text, an invoice is a row of numbers: its amount, how long the shop has been a customer, how often it paid late. Our made-up Nile Valley Foods model reads those features and gives each invoice a score between zero and one.

Here are the real scores for nine hundred test invoices, the ones held back and never used for learning. Grey bars are paid on time, eight hundred and seventeen of them. Red bars are paid late, eighty-three. Late invoices tend to score higher, but the groups overlap, like the two curves for the alarm.

The dashed lines are three thresholds. Move one and the errors trade places.

title.text:
The confusion matrix for the
invoice model at threshold 0.20

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_confusion_7.70x4.80_05527d63.png
objects.alt: The confusion matrix for the invoice model at threshold 0.20

objects.text: Real run. Positive means predicted late (score 0.20 or more).

runs.text: F1 = 38%. The 48 false negatives cost most.

slides.notes:
Put the line at zero point two. The model flags a hundred and two invoices as probably late. Thirty-five really were late: true positives. Sixty-seven were false positives, false alarms. Forty-eight late invoices were missed: false negatives. And seven hundred and fifty on-time invoices were rightly left alone: true negatives.

Two calculations by hand, with the same formulas as the alarm. Precision is true positives over true positives plus false positives: thirty-five over a hundred and two, thirty-four percent. Recall is true positives over true positives plus false negatives: thirty-five over eighty-three, forty-two percent. Which box would hurt your business most, the false positives or the false negatives?

title.text:
The invoice model must beat two baselines:
the majority class and a simple rule

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_baselines_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The invoice model must beat two baselines: the majority class and a simple rule

objects.text: 817 of 900 test invoices were on time: always saying on time scores 90.8%.

runs.text: Rule, paid late last year: precision 15%, recall 78%.

slides.notes:
With the matrix in hand, what must the invoice model beat?

The majority-class baseline predicts on time for every invoice. It is right eight hundred and seventeen times out of nine hundred, ninety point eight percent, and catches no late invoice. The second baseline is a plain rule a clerk could write: flag any shop that paid late at least once last year.

That rule catches seventy-eight percent of the late invoices, but it flags four hundred and forty-five invoices to find sixty-five, so only fifteen percent of its flags are right. Our model at a threshold of zero point two catches forty-two percent, with thirty-four percent of its flags right. If a vendor shows no baseline, ask for one.

title.text:
The same model at six thresholds: recall
climbs while precision and accuracy fall

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_thresholds_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The same model at six thresholds: recall climbs while precision and accuracy fall

objects.text: Recorded run, 6 Nov 2026: 900 test invoices, 83 late. Top row: majority-class baseline.

slides.notes:
Here is what moving that line does to every number we have met. This is the result table from the recorded run, and it is the one to study. Each row is the same model with a different threshold. At zero point five the model flags only nine invoices, catches six, and misses seventy-seven.

At zero point zero five it flags five hundred and twenty-six, and misses only five. Look down the recall column: seven, eighteen, forty-two, fifty-two, sixty-five, ninety-four percent. Now look at accuracy. It falls from ninety-one to fifty percent, which is worse than the majority-class baseline in the top row.

This is the second way a model looks good without being good: one number that hides the threshold.

title.text:
Demonstration 1: move the
threshold and read the row

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_9ba607ff.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 1: move the threshold and read the row

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Accuracy gets worse while recall improves.
The cheapest row depends on the costs.

slides.notes:
You do not have to take the table on trust, so I will run it in front of you. I open a terminal and type the threshold script with three values, zero point five, zero point two and zero point zero five. It rebuilds the same made-up dataset and the same model every time, because the random seeds are fixed, so you should see the numbers from the table.

Watch three things. Recall climbs as the threshold falls. Precision falls. And accuracy gets worse while recall improves. I will also change the cost figures and run again, so you can see that the best row changes with what a mistake costs. If you want a value tried, tell me and I will type it.

title.text:
The ROC curve plots every threshold at
once, and AUC sums it up in one number

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_roc_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: The ROC curve plots every threshold at once, and AUC sums it up in one number

objects.text: ROC: receiver operating characteristic. AUC: area under the curve. Each dot is a threshold.

runs.text: At 0.20: true positive rate 35 of 83 (42%), false positive rate 67 of 817 (8%).
AUC 0.80: a late invoice outscores an on-time one 80 times in 100.

slides.notes:
What did you see as the threshold fell?

Recall climbed, precision fell, accuracy got worse. The ROC curve draws that as one picture, one point for every threshold, as every sensitivity setting gives one point for the alarm. Up the side is the true positive rate, which is recall: true positives over true positives plus false negatives.

Along the bottom is the false positive rate: false positives over false positives plus true negatives. At a threshold of zero point two the point sits at thirty-five of eighty-three, forty-two percent, and sixty-seven of eight hundred and seventeen, eight percent. The dashed line is a coin flip.

The area under the curve is the AUC, here zero point eight. Pick one late and one on-time invoice, and about eighty times in a hundred the late one scores higher. AUC cannot choose your threshold, so what can?

title.text:
Choose the threshold with money: the best
line depends on what each mistake costs

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_cost_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Choose the threshold with money: the best line depends on what each mistake costs

objects.text: Assumed costs: UGX 20,000 per flag, UGX 300,000 per false negative.

slides.notes:
AUC cannot pick the line, but money can. This is where a finance manager feels at home. Suppose chasing a flagged invoice costs UGX 20,000 of staff time, and a missed late invoice costs UGX 300,000 in tied-up cash and follow-up. Those two figures are only my assumption, and you would use your own.

The formula: total cost equals flags times the chase cost, plus false negatives times the miss cost. Flags are true positives plus false positives, since staff chase every flag. At zero point two: a hundred and two flags times UGX 20,000 is UGX 2.04 million, plus forty-eight times UGX 300,000, which is UGX 14.4 million.

Total UGX 16.44 million. Never flagging costs UGX 24.9 million. With these costs the cheapest row is the lowest threshold. Change the costs and the answer changes.

title.text:
Overfitting on real data: the deeper the tree, the
better on the training set and the worse on the test set

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_memorise_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Overfitting on real data: the deeper the tree, the better on the training set and the worse on the test set

objects.text: A decision tree with more questions fits its training set more closely.

runs.text: On 900 test invoices: 85.2%, below the 90.8% baseline.

slides.notes:
So far we judged the model on invoices it had never studied, and that was deliberate. Now the real example of overfitting. We trained decision trees, the kind you met last time, with different depths. A depth is how many yes or no questions the tree may chain together.

The black line is the score on the two thousand one hundred training invoices. It climbs to a hundred percent. The red line is the score on the nine hundred test invoices it never saw. It falls to eighty-five point two percent, below the majority-class baseline at ninety point eight.

Like the spam filter, the deep tree has memorised its training set, accidents included. This is the third way a model looks good without being good.

title.text:
Demonstration 2: a deep tree
overfits, and the baseline shows it

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_versus_7.30x3.90_efe84b90.png
objects.alt: Demonstration 2: a deep tree overfits, and the baseline shows it

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: A small tree, depth 3: 91.1% training, 90.1% test.

slides.notes:
Let me show you that overfitting in the real output. I run the measuring script from the demo folder. It prints the baselines, the threshold table and the trees. Look for the deep tree: twenty-one questions deep, two hundred and twenty-nine leaves, a hundred percent on the training invoices.

Then look at the test score, eighty-five point two. Next to it, the majority-class baseline scores ninety point eight. A small tree, three questions deep, scores ninety-one percent on training invoices and ninety on test invoices, which is honest but no better than doing nothing. The lesson: ask for the score on the test set, and for the baseline beside it.

title.text: Which mistake costs more depends on the job

rows.text: A fine or a lost licence

objects.text: Equal costs are rare. Say which mistake hurts more before you choose a threshold.

slides.notes:
Both demonstrations say the same thing: a single number cannot tell you whether a model is good. What matters is what each mistake costs, and that changes with the job. In finance, a false negative, a missed late invoice, ties up cash, while a false positive costs a phone call.

In compliance, a missed suspicious payment can cost a fine, and a false alarm costs an analyst an hour. In customer service, a missed unhappy customer can be a lost shop. In HR, a missed strong candidate is a loss you never see. In operations, a missed breakdown costs a day of deliveries.

In legal work, a privileged document handed over by mistake is serious, while a lawyer reading one extra costs minutes. Which row is closest to your work?

title.text:
Twenty real cases from the test set: the
model flags a case at a score of 0.20 or more

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_cases_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Twenty real cases from the test set: the model flags a case at a score of 0.20 or more

objects.text: Drawn from the recorded run. Gold shows the invoices that really were paid late.

slides.notes:
You have the ideas, so now it is your turn with a pencil. This is your exercise sheet. It lists twenty invoices drawn from the real test set of the recorded run. For each one you see the invoice number, the amount, the score the model gave it, and whether it really was paid late, shown in gold.

Six of the twenty were late. The rule for the model is simple: a score of zero point two or more means positive, flagged. Read down the list once before you start, and notice that some late invoices score very low. Those will be false negatives. Then you fill in the confusion matrix and work out precision and recall.

title.text:
Fill the confusion matrix from the twenty
cases, then work out precision and recall

objects.text: 20 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Count the twenty cases into the four cells.

runs.text: Flag every case with a score of 0.20 or more.
Count TP, FP, FN and TN. They add to 20.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t03_blank_5.50x3.55.png
objects.alt: A blank two by two confusion matrix with the precision and recall formulas

objects.text: You keep: The filled matrix and two percentages. The worksheet.

slides.notes:
Here is what you do with those twenty cases. Take twenty minutes. Work alone or in pairs, with a pencil and the worksheet. First, go down the list and mark every case with a score of zero point two or more as flagged. Second, count the four cells: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

They must add up to twenty, which is your check. Third, work out precision as true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. Fourth, work out recall as true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. Write each as a fraction first, then as a percentage.

I will walk round. When you have finished, compare with your neighbour and ask why any answers differ.

title.text:
Move the threshold by hand: raise
it to 0.50, then lower it to 0.15

objects.text: 5 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Redo the counts at two new thresholds.

runs.text: Cross out your flags and flag again at 0.50.
Fill the first row of the small table.
Say which threshold you would choose, and why.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_3f07784e.png
objects.alt: A small table to fill in at three thresholds, with the 0.20 row already done

objects.text: You keep: Two rows of the table and one sentence.

slides.notes:
Keep your answers, because the same twenty cases give you a second exercise of five minutes. Change the threshold in your head. First raise it to zero point five and recount. Fill in the first row of the small table. Then lower it to zero point fifteen and fill in the third row.

The middle row, zero point two, is already done from your last exercise, so you can check yourself against it. I walk round again. Look at what happens to precision and recall as the threshold moves. Then write one sentence saying which threshold you would choose for a late-payment model, and what it would cost you in false positives or false negatives.

title.text:
Six questions to put to any
vendor about the numbers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_folder_0.69.png

objects.text: What test data was it measured on? Had it seen it?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_flag_0.69.png

objects.text: How common is the case? What does the majority class score?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_switch_0.69.png

objects.text: What are precision and recall, at which threshold?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.69.png

objects.text: Who chose the threshold? What did each mistake cost?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_people_0.69.png

objects.text: How does it compare with a simple rule or today?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.69.png

objects.text: Can we test it on 50 of our own cases?

slides.notes:
You have now done by hand what a vendor's single number hides, so here is what to ask. When a vendor says, our model is ninety-five percent accurate, you now have six questions. What test data was that measured on, and had the model seen it?

How common is the thing you are looking for, and what would the majority-class baseline score?

What are precision and recall, and at which threshold?

Who chose the threshold, and what did each kind of mistake cost?

How does it compare with a simple rule or with how we do it today?

And can we test it on fifty of our own cases before we sign?

The full one-page sheet has four more, about monitoring, drift and who checks.

title.text:
Which mistake would cost your business
more: a false positive or a false negative?

objects.text: Think of the task you would most like a model to help with. Which mistake costs more?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.80.png

objects.text: A false negative
Set the threshold low. Accept more false positives. Ask for recall.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_check_0.80.png

objects.text: A false positive
Set the threshold high. Ask for precision.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_chart_0.80.png

objects.text: About equal
Balance them. Ask for F1 and the threshold used.

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_coin_0.80.png

objects.text: I do not know yet
Put a UGX figure on each mistake first.
Write the task, the costlier mistake and a first UGX figure for each in your workbook.

slides.notes:
In the exercise you saw that the best threshold moves with the cost of each mistake, so bring that back to your own work. Think of one task you would like a model to help with: an alert, a shortlist, a sort. Ask yourself which mistake costs more, a false positive or a false negative.

If a false negative costs more, you want the threshold low and you should ask the vendor for recall. If a false positive costs more, set it high and ask for precision. If they are about equal, ask for F1 and the threshold. And if you do not know, that is the finding: put a UGX figure on each mistake before you buy anything. Say your answer aloud to the group.
